summary: Describes a set of mappings between X.400 mail systems and systems using the RFC 822 mail format. X.400 was a CCITT standard for store-and-forward messaging, and these mappings let the two worlds interwork. It was a proposed protocol, was updated by RFC 1026, RFC 1138 and RFC 1148, and was replaced by RFC 1327 and RFC 2156.

eli5.summary: Two countries use different postal forms. This memo is the translation table that lets a letter written on one form be understood when it arrives in the other.

subtitle: The first rulebook for gateways that translate email between X.400 systems and RFC 822 Internet mail.

tldr.problem: Large communities used RFC 822 mail while X.400 was expected to be widely implemented, and the two use different address and message formats.
tldr.mechanism: A gateway maps X.400 addresses and protocol elements to RFC 822 addresses and header fields and back, using encoded O/R names, domain defined attributes and some new RFC 822 headers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 987 was updated by RFC 1026, RFC 1138 and RFC 1148, and replaced by RFC 1327 and RFC 2156.

today: RFC 987 was updated by RFC 1026, RFC 1138 and RFC 1148, and was replaced by RFC 1327 and RFC 2156. Those later RFCs are where the X.400 to RFC 822 mapping continued.

sections.title: Two Mail Worlds and a Gateway
sections.content:
RFC 987 describes mappings that let systems running the CCITT X.400 (1984) protocols interwork with systems using the RFC 822 mail format or protocols derived from it. The approach aims to maximise the services offered across the boundary without unduly complex mappings, and should not require any changes to end systems.

The RFC says RFC 822 mail was used on the ARPA-Internet with SMTP, and also on UUCP networks, CSNET, BITNET and the JNT Mail networks. The mappings suit all of these. Several gateways, sometimes called mail relays, were expected, and a common specification lets them behave consistently, which matters most when a message passes through more than one.

Its principles are to stay pragmatic, to keep functionality across the gateway as high as possible, and not to lose information in the conversion. It considers only the X.400 Interpersonal Messaging Service (P2), carried over the Message Transfer Service (P1). Other kinds of message are rejected at the gateway.
sections.eli5: Some people write letters in one style and some in another. A gateway is a translator in the middle who tries not to lose any words.

sections.title: Which Services Survive the Trip
sections.content:
Chapter 2 goes through the end-user services of each system and says how far a gateway can support them. A service counts as supported when it maps with matching meaning, no loss of information, and any required action.

Many RFC 822 header fields map straight across: Date:, From:, Sender:, Reply-To:, To:, Cc:, Bcc:, Message-Id:, References: and Subject:. Others, such as Keywords:, Comments:, Encrypted:, Resent-* and unknown fields like X-*, are passed in the message text.

Going the other way, the RFC does not push X.400 elements into the body. Instead it defines new RFC 822 headers, expected to be registered, for things such as the converted indication, the importance and sensitivity indications, and the expiry date. Some elements are not supported, including receipt and non-receipt notification and body part encryption.
sections.eli5: Some parts of a letter, like who it is from and what it is about, translate easily. Special notes with no match in the other language get tucked into the message itself so nothing is lost.

sections.title: Basic Encodings
sections.content:
X.400 is encoded in a structured binary form, while RFC 822 is text, so chapter 3 defines how to write X.400 values as text. A gateway treats IA5 as ASCII. Booleans become TRUE or FALSE, and numeric strings are digits.

The X.400 PrintableString character set lacks several characters common in mail addresses. The RFC therefore defines special escapes: (a) for @, (p) for %, (b) for !, (q) for the double quote and (u) for the underscore. Any other ASCII character can be written as ( followed by three decimal digits and ). The mapping is deliberately asymmetric, and the RFC admits it does not try to minimise the number of pathological cases.

Timestamps map symmetrically between UTCTime and the RFC 822 date-time syntax. T.61 strings, meant for humans, follow the CEN/CENELEC mappings.
sections.eli5: Some letters and symbols are not allowed in one kind of mail, so the translator writes them with short codes, such as writing the at-sign as (a).

sections.title: Mapping Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC calls addressing probably the trickiest problem of the gateway. An X.400 address is an O/R name, a set of attribute and value pairs such as country (C), administration domain (ADMD), private domain (PRMD), organisation (O), organisational unit (OU) and personal name parts. The RFC defines a textual form, for example /PN=J.Linnimouth/GQ=5/, and a personal name shorthand such as Marshall.Rose or M.T.Rose.

Because the two worlds are not fully symmetric, the mapping works in two directions. An X.400 address can be encoded in the local part and domain of an RFC 822 address, with a table linking domains to O/R name attributes (for example, the domain AC.UK could be associated with a country, ADMD and PRMD). Going the other way, a genuine RFC 822 address is carried inside an X.400 address as a domain defined attribute of type RFC-822, JNT-Mail or UUCP.

When an RFC 822 address cannot be read as an X.400 encoding, an RFC 822 recipient must be rejected, but return addresses and header addresses are wrapped in the domain defined attribute instead. The RFC notes that the syntax may be used to source route, and gives an appendix format for sharing the domain tables between gateways.
sections.eli5: X.400 addresses are like a list of labels (country, company, person), while Internet addresses are a name at a place. The translator turns one into the other, and tucks the other kind of address inside a label when it cannot be translated.

sections.title: Mapping Messages and Reports
sections.content:
Chapter 5 gives the field-by-field mappings. For RFC 822 to X.400, the header fields build a P1 envelope and a P2 heading. The body goes into an IA5 text body part. If any headers have no X.400 equivalent, a first body part starting with the line RFC-822-Headers: holds them in their original order. Examples of the mappings include To: to the primary recipients, Cc: to the copy recipients and Subject: to the subject.

For X.400 to RFC 822, a gateway builds a pro-forma message. A probe is serviced by the gateway itself since RFC 822 has no equivalent. A delivery report becomes an RFC 822 message from an administrator at the gateway, with new headers such as Delivery-Report-Content-Original for the report details.

Return of contents is handled in one of two ways, depending on how widely X.400 systems support it. Where it is not widely supported, the gateway tracks delivery reports itself and sends a timeout failure notice to the originator if no report comes back.
sections.eli5: When a letter is translated, each part of it goes to the matching slot. Parts with no slot go into a note at the top of the message so the reader still sees them.

sections.title: Where It Fits and What Followed
sections.content:
The memo calls itself a proposed protocol for the ARPA-Internet community. It says it should be used when this mapping is performed on the ARPA-Internet or in the UK Academic Community, and that it may be modified in the light of implementation experience although no substantial changes are expected.

The appendices cover details for specific mail systems: JNT Mail, Internet mail, Phonenet mail and UUCP mail, plus the format of the address mapping tables.
sections.eli5: This was a first draft of the translation rules, meant to be improved after people tried it.
